response: HTTP/2 removed HoL blocking at the HTTP layer only. TCP still has it at the transport level. Packet loss on one stream blocks all others. HTTP/3 uses QUIC (UDP-based), which multiplexes streams independently, eliminating transport-level HoL blocking.

No. Cluster-admin gives every service full cluster permissions. Any compromise spreads across your entire cluster. Single namespace removes network policy isolation boundaries. This creates a blast radius that grows as services proliferate, even now. Separate namespaces plus per-service service accounts plus network policies take about 30 minutes to set up and deliver value immediately.

RAID is not backup. RAID protects against hardware failure. Delete a file and RAID mirrors the deletion. Encrypt your data and RAID encrypts the copies. Backup is an independent copy. External drive, separate system, different location.

MongoDB is not standard for financial ledgers. Financial systems use ACID-compliant relational databases. PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server. Double-entry bookkeeping requires atomic writes across multiple ledger entries. MongoDB's document model adds complexity. Use a relational DB with transaction support, append-only ledger table, and audit triggers.

Kafka doesn't delete messages when read. Messages stay in the topic partition until retention period expires (default 7 days, configurable). Each consumer reads independently from its offset. Multiple services can consume the same topic. Each maintains its own offset position.

Write in isolation and you risk finishing three chapters before learning your thesis doesn't land or your structure fails. Test one rough chapter with 2-3 target readers first, incorporate feedback, commit to the full outline. You'll save time and write stronger.

The 200k is already spent. It doesn't change the math on whether to continue. The question is whether finishing costs more than the value it delivers. If yes, stop. If no, continue. Using 'we already invested this' as a reason to continue is backward reasoning.

Standups are not universally agreed to be wasteful. Some teams use them effectively for blocker discovery and quick alignment. Others do them poorly. Before replacing them, try: time-box to 5 minutes, focus on blockers and dependencies, move solutions to separate discussions. If still wasteful after that, reevaluate.
